I guess I am not, and never will be, a shotgun type trader - try many setups, win 50% for 3R or more. There's nothing wrong with it, and it's a great way to make money, but I just have difficulty pulling the trigger on anything if I'm not 90% sure.

Just 1 trade today, I waited 3 hours for the planets to align - there was a really nice confluence on EURX/USDX that I'd been waiting all morning for (if anyone is interested I'll post it up - but it will require another 4 charts to properly explain).

This high probability currency index confluence was what gave me the 90% certainty I needed to enter EU long at these levels, with heavy lot.

As it happened, USDX only sold off a bit and then chopped, and it was in fact mainly EURX strength which was pulling EU upwards. The real move was on the GBPX selloff at the same time, so EG flew northwards whilst mine chopped towards TG.

I won't lie, I lost my nerve and did not hold for my full TG. Full TG was the small gap close at pole base (gaps which don't actually exist if you listen to some...) I have a profit target of 10-15% daily, and when you have open trades worth over 10%, and price is chopping your direction, it is difficult to hold. As such, I closed early for about 11% account gain. If I'd have held full positions to full TG, it would have been about 20% (although price is still not there yet).

Still, this is much more my style - sniper rather than shotgun. I only needed this one trade, although I had to wait 3 hours for it to setup, and I was 90% certain of the result. I am now finished for the day and will go relax into the weekend.
EG and EU shorts taken this morning with EURX/GBPX/USDX confluence.

They don't always work... Made a bit of a mess of waiting for the correct confluence levels on the currency indexes so got in a bit soon on EG. Managed to scratch both for tiny loss, no big deal. There should be another sell opportunity soon.

Turned out the EG trade was good, but I wasn't going to mess around - price broke my entry level and gave me a chance to get out, I've been burned too many times to risk it.

Bunch of other small scalps, NU long last trade I'm going to take today. Talk about taking profit at the right time!

You can see from many of my trades, if you have got the ability to analyse levels and price structures on M1, it's really not too hard to generate 4R or more over 15-20 pips.
Impressive, I must say.

Been a while since I checked in. I'd like to tell you I'm a millionaire, but I can't! Still struggling to find consistency on live. I am plagued by emotional poor decision making still, and finding it very difficult to overcome. I'm trying to implement more and more rules in my trading to help overcome this. I'll get there eventually I'm sure.

Just wanted to post an example of how it is becoming more difficult to read bigger moves on price. This is M15 UJ PA from the last few days. We had a clear strong reaction to a valid zone, what appeared to be an engulf south, and then price just came right back up and engulfed the original zone.

i.imgur.com/8Moo2KF.png

In these conditions of increasing numbers of fakeouts, even when coming off valid levels, it brings home the importance of hitting these nice zones accurately FTB, and then really maximising the profit you take from the first strong surge of price in your favour. As time goes on, and more PA unfolds away from the initial reaction, the picture becomes muddier and muddier.

Yeah I don't I see it. In terms of important FLs/FTRs, there was an engulf south.
The only way I can explain it is that it was reacting to the big FL below, and that price can reverse anywhere in a FL. But this is conflicting with my understanding of fractals.

Yes price has to turn from "something" fractal on a lower timeframe inside a higher timeframe FL. Something being an important FL/QM etc on a smaller scale.

FOs can be expected when there is a continuation engulf in play - for instance, if the supply level had been engulfed north already at the top of the move down, then the FO wouldn't have surprised me as much. But FO when reacting to a valid level is just unfair

This simply looks like a case of "rules being broken" to me, unless someone can come up with a compelling reason why it turned there.

First; be very clear where you are anticipating price is moving from and where it is going to on some HTF. Here's my guess. No compelling reason to hold onto shorts at this stage, at the very least, take some profit off the table if you were in short.

Second; price will always whipsaw and overshoot levels on the LTF against a HTF analysis whether that be LTF M15/HTF D1 or LTF D1/HTF MN. Given the background of long bias created in the Daily chart, where might the best opportunities for buying occur? Where there has previously been buying..Either widen your stop, or be prepared to have multiple stabs at a setup, or identify potential obstacles to take profit if you're in the opposite direction.

Thanks for the thoughts Shadow.

I was looking for price to complete the short move from the H1 zone to a valid bullish level before continuing north - but as always, it's best not to try to base an entire trade decision off a single piece of information (the "engulf" I thought I'd seen), as you point out.

It's frustrating many times to have a set of rules (FLs, engulfs etc) which work *most* of the time (and enable you to make highly accurate predictions of what price is going to do next on every timeframe) - and then there is 20% of the time where they just don't work at all, and completely throw you off track on to the wrong decision.

But as they say - rules are made to be broken.

I'm a serial LTF addict, always got my head stuck in M1/M5/M15. I don't step outside these timeframes enough still for the bigger picture.

Encouragingly, I'm getting better and better now at finding amazing trade setups, over and over. and really understanding and reading the various price cycles. I can usualy open up a chart and eyeball a massive price turn level within 30 seconds. I utterly suck at running trades however!

I have ingrained scalping into my psyche so much over the last 18 months, that it causes me almost unbearable mental anguish to try to hold a trade longer than 30 minutes. I honestly don't know what to do with myself, my brain is just screaming at me to take the profit, or close the thing out if price takes too long to start moving in my favour.

Nothing for it but to just force myself to overcome it, bit by bit.

Cheers

Away

hi smimon, This is how I see!!

Yes maknill, you are correct. I had it in my mind that is was a "rule" that price was not allowed to do a continuation FO when it was coming off a valid HTF level - I thought continuation engulfs (FO of minor level and continue) could occur only when there was a HTF engulf in favour of the move in play - but I guess this is not a rule after all

There is a fine balance to be struck between application of a strict price model to enable us to make reasonable assumptions and predictions of price movement, but also when to understand that these are not set in stone and that rules can be bent (or sometimes broken totally).

Imagine a world with no FOs... how easy would all this be

If any of you are anything like me, you probably have markup on your charts all the time, showing zones of interest, marking where engulfs occurred, etc. Indeed, I've even written a ton of indicators to help me out with this, including a FlagLimit indicator which allows FLs to be defined on multiple scales, finds if they have been engulfed or not, monitors them for price proximity/enter/engulf etc.

Since I like to adopt a currency based approach to my trading, I trade all USD and EUR crosses, in conjunction with 7 currency indexes (I don't trade CHF crosses just because the spread on most of them is terrible (apart from ECHF and UCHF) and because the index confluence doesn't work too well). This means I've got over 15 charts open across 2 instances of MT4, all with marked zones and alerts on them. At any given time, especially in times of high volatility in the markets, there are alerts going off every 2 minutes. You can have been waiting patiently for a setup, and watching price, and suddenly another 4 alerts go off, and your concentration is pulled all over the place. My head is a mess, my thinking is muddled.

I am also guilty of having a proximity alert to one of my zones go off, and then just thinking "I'll go stare at something else, and wait for the alert to go off that price has actually entered the zone before I decide whether to hit it or not". As a result, when price does enter the zone, I've not been paying attention, and I am out of tune with the approach, the speed of it, the way the candles are forming etc, and I tend to just make a rushed hasty decision to hit the level without a second thought. Sometimes it's fine if I've analysed the zone correctly, sometimes it goes instantly wrong as I've misjudged the strength of the move.

Also, whether you are aware of it or not, the second you place a single piece of markup on your charts, a single line, box, whatever - your thinking is influenced from that point forwards. Every time you look at that chart, you are starting with a single default assumption based on your markup, and everything subsequently is viewed through this lens. If your markup is valid and accurate - great; but if it's not, everything you try to trade from that point forwards will be biased towards being incorrect. Think - how many times have you drawn a zone, and then later in the day some more price action plays out, and you realised it was totally incorrect?

All of this is to say - less is more.

I've realised that the only thing holding me back from consistent success (my equity is up and down like a yo-yo at present) is my mental approach and organisation. I need a clear mind, need to be able to focus, need to be reading price clearly every time I sit down and not base my thinking on a load of assumptions I made 2 days ago.

To this end, I now only set alerts on my currency index charts (crosspairs don't usually make turns until the relevant currency index is at the correct level anyway), and at the start of every day, I wipe every single object off my charts. This cleaning of the charts has 2 benefits - it not only makes sure you are really reading what's going on with no previous assumptions, it also over time will dramatically improve your speed of analysis by eye, until you get to the point where you can just eyeball a chart and know pretty much what's going on in under 10 seconds, and where the next likely levels in play will be. I also now do not allow myself to use "zone entered" alerts - if I receive a proximity alert for a zone, i turn everything else off, and force myself to stare at that chart until the setup plays out.

You can glean a lot more information out of a naked chart than a chart with 43 boxes and lines all over it. Don't forget, the manner in which price is moving (surging, driving, compressing, flagging etc) is one of the biggest clues we have as to future intent, or whether what we think is an engulf is actually a FO. Yoy simple cannot see this piece of information clearly with clutter everywhere.

I do this too. I can almost never use levels I have from the previous day(with the exception of very HTF levels), and it's a bit frustrating and adds time to the process in the morning before work.. but I usually can't trade successfully off old levels. Even though I'll wipe the chart, and usually come up w/ the exact same levels. But some part of the mental process of marking it up that day makes a difference in how well you can read price, for me anyway.

The exception to this is if on the lower time frame I'm looking at one specific level for a trade. For example, an FTR trade, if I mark it up the night before and I have the level/FL engulfed, and the FTR zone. and nothing else. Then I can re-use that. But other than that, I'd need to wipe the chart and start again.

Art wrote:

nsamaroo wrote: I'd need to wipe the chart and start again.

As I mentioned in my comment, I actually feel it's of benefit to mark up blank charts from scratch over and over again. Every time you do it, you get quicker and quicker, and you start noticing more and more things which explain price turns which you might not have noticed previously. Eventually, you don't even really need any markup on your charts at all, you are just able to eyeball what's going on and what levels are in play. (at some times of course it's still going to be necessary to drop down to LTF and draw some stuff to refine accuracy of levels etc).

Well, a nice end to the week. I have been treading water on live for nearly 6 months now, in an endless cycle of boom and bust. Every bust is caused by me getting mad and doubling and trebling down on losing trades. But I'm seeing improvement in my mental approach. My chart skills are not the issue at this stage

EU faked some HTF lows off the news, and I saw the initial M1 candle get rejected all the way back up to the top, then closed down at the low as it was forming - this was a pretty good sign that a reversal was occurring. I waited for a clean engulfing surge, and then tried to gauge the depth of the retracement. One of my strongest skills is PA reading during times of high volatility, I just find it laughably easy because everything is so exaggerated.

In these cases, I look for what I've seen referred to as a "key reversal" bar (KR) in order to confirm that the current LTF swing is about to reverse. A KR bar (let's say a bullish one), has a low outside the current range, but closes right back up high into the range, with almost no top wick. As with all PA, it has to happen at a level which makes sense.

I waited for the KR bar, entered with SL just below it, and targeted the area of the origin of the last swing down on HTF, and walked away from the PC - because I know if I sit there and stare at it, I will meddle. End result was a nice 23R trade in a little over an hour.

EU M1

Here is a close up of the KR bar. In this case, I used the z-line of the cluster that formed after the news retracement as my "level to make the PA make sense".

Ah dudu, a typically constructive post delivered in your usual eloquent manner.

If anyone needs a translation I believe what dudu is trying to say is "I am surprised you are not having consistent returns. I tried RTM for a while, but could not find consistency with the method, so I returned to a simpler method of trading."

Well, it's a valid point. I've seen a lot of people come and go just over the last year on here, initially excited by the prospect of making 0 pip entries, and then leaving in frustration some time later, usually cursing IF. Let me say a few things in response.

First, the freely available material on RTM is NOT going to teach you how to make 0 pip entries. That would be madness to give away for nothing. What is does teach you are the concepts which you need to know, and apply over and over again, in order to develop your own understanding to the point where you can make 0 pip trades. Believe me, I've done it myself a large number of times by now. As IF has said, he has also given enough hints without spelling it out directly. I put together what he has said on here, and especially over at the FF thread, and figured out how he does it, and have been able to replicate it to a lesser extent. He's still much better at it than me though

Second, the reason I am not consistent has nothing to do with RTM, it's entirely my own fault. For me, trading is 25% skill, 75% mental control. I'm overconfident and impatient by nature and I hate to lose - I think it's not too hard to see why this is an awful combination for trading. Every time I sit down, I'm not only analysing charts, I'm also trying to fight my base personality. I hit far too many unconfirmed entries at dodgy levels, I boredom scalp, I use too much risk, I revenge trade.

But you see the difference between dudu and I, is that when I am failing to find consistency with a method that others are employing successfully, instead of cursing the system and the mentor who gave us the concepts. I assume ownership of my failure, and admit that the reason I'm not succeeding is due to my own failings. This is something we call intellectual honesty

Of course, the other option is to protect your ego, and tell yourself some pretty lie that the reason you didn't succeed with a proven method is not because you personally failed to apply it properly, but because the teacher is "BS".

Don't forget people - trading is HARD. There is pretty much zero chance you're going to pick this up and run with consistent profits in less than 12 months, at an absolute minimum. Sure, you can gain the analysis skills in much less time than that, but learning to control your own mental state and fight those elements of your brain that are constantly striving to sabotage you - well, that's the real battle, and that's what takes years of endless repetition. You also need this amount of time to really develop that "feel" for price, which cannot be quantified.

I've added 1000% to my account over a 12 day period. I've added 100% to my account even in a single day. But then I've gone on a madness revenge spiral and given it all back, or blown my account with a single stupid trade with no SL, which I kept adding to all the way.

As soon as I can stop self-sabotaging, my consistent returns and large sums of money are waiting for me. The only variable in the equation I still need to solve is me

It is not a post. It is a gold nugget here.

Smimom, I salute you. I have same understanding of trading. Issues lie in ME

I never increased risk. Though occasionally take revenge trade or two. Worst issue of mine is pulling of trades without confirmation (or I talk myself into lousy confirmations), choose odd locations to trade etc.

Not sure one can do about it.. the only thing that makes sense is to get back at it every single day, write down issues, pay more and more attention what is happening inside the head while trading, marking levels etc.

Some things that make a difference in my trading: 1. If I mark up charts when I'm calm -results are good (if I do charts when in rush, wife is angry, have to run to meeting etc results are very bad). 2. Re-doing charts daily as per Smimom's previous posts makes a tremendious difference.
